findings.source_passage: there was one persistent story that he didn't live in a house at all, but in a boat that looked like a house and was moved secretly up and down the Long Island shore
findings.why_it_matters: This specific legend is part of the novel's texture of rumor and mythology surrounding Gatsby — the floating-house detail is distinctive and contributes to the sense of his uncanny, ungrounded existence. Its removal flattens the inventory of legends.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the boat-house legend alongside the 'underground pipeline to Canada' detail; both fit in the same sentence and cost almost nothing in word count.

findings.source_passage: The none too savoury ramifications by which Ella Kaye, the newspaper woman, played Madame de Maintenon to his weakness and sent him to sea in a yacht, were common property of the turgid journalism in 1902.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is rhetorically distinctive — the Madame de Maintenon allusion, 'turgid journalism,' and the precise 1902 date establish Fitzgerald's ironic-historical register and fix Cody as a Gilded Age type. Its removal strips interpretive context from the Ella Kaye plot and flattens the prose style.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Ella Kaye / Madame de Maintenon sentence; it is a single sentence with high stylistic and contextual yield.

findings.source_passage: Sometimes in the course of gay parties women used to rub champagne into his hair; for himself he formed the habit of letting liquor alone.
findings.source_locator: paragraph following the Cody portrait description
findings.why_it_matters: This detail is memorable and interpretively important — it explains Gatsby's famous sobriety at his own parties and ties it causally to the Cody episode. The draft retains only the bare statement that Cody influenced Gatsby's drinking, losing the vivid, ironic image.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the champagne-in-the-hair sentence; it takes one line and supplies the novel's explanation for Gatsby's abstemiousness.

findings.source_passage: It is invariably saddening to look through new eyes at things upon which you have expended your own powers of adjustment.
findings.source_locator: paragraph introducing Tom and Daisy's arrival at Gatsby's party
findings.why_it_matters: This aphoristic sentence is critically engaged — it is Nick at his most essayistic and is routinely quoted as a meditation on perspective and disillusionment. The draft includes it verbatim, which is correct — noting this as preserved.

findings.source_passage: She was appalled by West Egg, this unprecedented 'place' that Broadway had begotten upon a Long Island fishing village—appalled by its raw vigour that chafed under the old euphemisms and by the too obtrusive fate that herded its inhabitants along a shortcut from nothing to nothing.
findings.source_locator: after the director-and-star scene, before Nick sits on the front steps
findings.why_it_matters: While the draft does include this passage, it omits the crucial interpretive frame that precedes it in the source: 'But the rest offended her—and inarguably because it wasn't a gesture but an emotion.' The draft does retain this line, so the passage is present. However, the draft drops the entire intervening scene — Daisy singing with the music ('in a husky, rhythmic whisper, bringing out a meaning in each word that it had never had before and would never have again') — displacing it to after Tom's bootlegger exchange rather than in its source position contextualizing Daisy's emotional state before her departure. The singing passage is signature prose and is misplaced in the draft, weakening its interpretive function.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Daisy's singing passage to its source position — immediately after Tom's party socializing, before the front-steps departure scene — so it functions as the emotional pivot Fitzgerald intended, not as an afterthought following Tom's 'menagerie' line.

findings.source_passage: A lot of these newly rich people are just big bootleggers, you know… I didn't hear it. I imagined it.
findings.source_locator: Tom's bootlegger exchange on the front steps
findings.why_it_matters: Tom's 'I didn't hear it. I imagined it' reply is rhetorically sharp and character-defining — it shows Tom's aggressive class contempt cloaked as offhand wit. The draft reduces the exchange to 'Not Gatsby,' losing this exchange entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Tom's 'I didn't hear it. I imagined it. A lot of these newly rich people are just big bootleggers, you know' — one sentence that defines Tom's posture toward Gatsby and sets up his later investigation.

findings.source_passage: Through all he said, even through his appalling sentimentality, I was reminded of something—an elusive rhythm, a fragment of lost words… what I had almost remembered was uncommunicable forever.
findings.why_it_matters: The closing paragraph is preserved verbatim, which is correct. Flagging as preserved; no issue here.

summary: The draft preserves most major passages but has one high-severity structural displacement (Daisy's singing scene misplaced), drops the Madame de Maintenon / Ella Kaye sentence, erases the champagne-in-the-hair detail, omits Tom's 'I imagined it' line, and loses the boat-house legend — collectively constituting a pattern of voice flattening and one high-severity finding that requires regeneration.
